n: In this lecture we study the 1,4-benzodiazepine derivatives. The section begins with general information, then considers isolation from physical evidence, and analysis by immunochemical and TLC screening methods. Key terms: tranquilliser, acid hydrolysis, benzophenone, the Izotov method, the Bratton-Marshall reaction, TLC, and UV, IR and mass spectra. The outline is as follows: first general information, then metabolism and poisoning, then the hydrolysis-benzophenone method, and finally the individual substances.

The first question: what is this group? The 1,4-benzodiazepine derivatives belong to the tranquillisers. In the early 1960s chlordiazepoxide was synthesised, and later diazepam, nitrazepam and oxazepam. The group has more than 2 thousand derivatives, of which 12-15 are widely used in medicine. Chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, oxazepam and nitrazepam have toxicological and narcological significance. That is, in practice it is these four substances that one most often has to deal with.

Now the narcological significance. The main effects are calming, that is tranquillising, and hypnotic activity. The drug relieves fear, anxiety, agitation and headache. In addition it has muscle-relaxant properties. Importantly, these substances potentiate the action of ethyl alcohol, narcotics, narcotic analgesics and hypnotic substances. For this reason, taking them together with other agents can be dangerous.

We turn to the question of action and dependence. The Polish researchers A. Welbel and others noted in 1984 that harmful and toxic effects of benzodiazepines are rarely seen. With chlordiazepoxide and phenazepam, muscle tone falls, while diazepam enhances the activity of muscle relaxants. However, with prolonged use the picture changes: the substance accumulates, and habituation and psychological and physical dependence are observed. So in the short term the harm is small, but with prolonged use there is a risk of dependence.

Let us consider the pharmacokinetics. The 1,4-benzodiazepines are rapidly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract. The half-life in blood is on average 1-2 days. Oxazepam reaches its maximum concentration within 4 hours and disappears from plasma by the end of the second day. It has been shown by gas chromatography that after diazepam is taken, its metabolites increase in plasma during the first and second weeks. Even when diazepam is taken for a long time at 2-4 times the usual dose, its plasma concentration remains low.

The metabolic pathways differ with the substance. Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide are broken down in the liver by N-demethylation, and desmethyldiazepam undergoes hydroxylation. Chlordiazepoxide also undergoes hydroxylation and dealkylation in the liver. Oxazepam, the N-demethylation product of diazepam, forms a water-soluble glucuronide with glucuronic acid and is excreted in the urine. Nitrazepam, by contrast, is reduced, and 20% of it is excreted in the urine as 7-amino and 7-acetylamino metabolites.

Poisoning and its clinical stages. Benzodiazepine derivatives are absorbed from the stomach and small intestine and bind to blood plasma proteins. In unconscious patients the substance can be found in the stomach even 2-3 days after it was taken. Poisoning has 3 clinical stages: the first is drowsiness and light sleep, the second is superficial coma, that is unconsciousness, and the third is loss of consciousness. If the loss of consciousness lasts more than 12 hours, bronchopneumonia, collapse, and hepatic and renal failure are observed.

Now the hydrolysis stage of the Izotov method. Analysis by hydrolysis products was proposed by B. N. Izotov, I. V. Volkova and others. The procedure is as follows: to 10 ml of urine or 2 ml of blood, 10 ml, or for blood 2 ml, of concentrated HCl is added and heated for 1 hour in a bath under a reflux condenser. Then the pH is brought to 8-10 with saturated NaOH, and the mixture is extracted twice with 10 ml of chloroform. Finally, it is evaporated and TLC follows.

As a result of hydrolysis, benzodiazepines are converted into benzophenones. Chlordiazepoxide gives ACB, that is 2-amino-5-chlorobenzophenone. Diazepam forms MCB, that is 2-methylamino-5-chlorobenzophenone. From nitrazepam, ANB is obtained, that is 2-amino-5-nitrobenzophenone, and from phenazepam, BCB. 2,5-Diaminobenzophenone, that is DAB, is also cited in connection with nitrazepam. Oxazepam, like chlordiazepoxide, forms ACB. For this reason, the type of substance can be inferred from the product.

t: Isolation from a biological specimen by Izotov
n: Isolation from a biological specimen by Izotov. The stomach, intestine, liver and kidney are taken as the specimen. The minced specimen is left with acidified water, at pH=2, for 1 hour. The aqueous extract is poured off and extracted with chloroform, and the chloroform layer is discarded. The aqueous layer is brought to pH=9-10 and extracted 3 times with diethyl ether. Then the ether is evaporated and the residue is dissolved in chloroform.

Detecting benzophenones by TLC. Benzene is used as the chromatographic system, and yellow spots of varying intensity appear on the plate. Then NaNO2, 0.1% HCl, 0.5% sulphanilic acid and a solution of naphthol in alkali are sprayed on. As a result, ACB turns red and ANB bright orange. MCB turns yellow, and sometimes the colour disappears. Besides colour, detection is also made by Rf values, which are given in Table 17.

t: Table 17: Rf and UV spectral maxima
n: Note Table 17. The DAB product of nitrazepam stays on the starting line. The remaining hydrolysis products differ in Rf and UV maximum. ANB, that is nitrazepam: Rf 0.17-0.18, UV maxima 238 and 358. BCB, that is phenazepam: Rf 0.43-0.45, maxima 230 and 400. MCB, that is diazepam: Rf 0.57, maxima 238 and 410. ACB, that is chlordiazepoxide: Rf 0.35-0.37, maxima 238 and 390.

Unchanged benzodiazepines can also be analysed directly by TLC. For this, silica gel of grade KSK or Silufol thin-layer plates are used. The solvent system consists of ethyl acetate, methyl alcohol and 25% ammonia solution in the ratio 85:10:5. The spots on the plate are visualised by spraying with Dragendorff reagent. That is, by this method we identify the substance without hydrolysis, as it is.

The first of the general reactions is the ninhydrin reaction. It should be said at the outset: the identification of 1,4-benzodiazepine derivatives has not been studied sufficiently, so the reactions below are regarded as general. Ninhydrin is added to the solution, which is heated on a water bath for 3 minutes. Then, when 5 ml of ethyl alcohol is added, the solution turns blue. After 2 drops of 1% copper sulphate solution are added, the colour changes first to red and then to brown.

Precipitating reagents are used for all benzodiazepines. A chloroform solution of the drug is dropped onto a microscope slide and the solvent is evaporated. To the residue, 1 drop of 0.1 N HCl is added, and after 5-10 minutes a drop of the reagent. Dragendorff reagent gives an amorphous precipitate or red crystals. The iron iodide complex forms dark brown rods in 15 minutes. A 0.8% alcoholic solution of iodine monochloride gives needle-shaped crystals, and after 45-60 minutes, prism-shaped ones. The copper iodide complex forms dark brown needles in 1 hour.

Quantitative analysis is based on the Bratton-Marshall method. In the photocolorimetric method a cherry-coloured product is formed. After hydrolysis with HCl, a 10% solution of NaNO2 is added to the cooled liquid and left for 3 minutes. Then 0.5 ml of a 0.5% solution of ammonium sulphamate is added and the mixture is left for another 3 minutes. After that, 0.5 ml of a 0.1% solution of naphthylethylenediamine dihydrochloride is added. The absorbance is compared with a standard solution on a PEC instrument, and the quantity is calculated from a calibration graph.

Now we turn to the individual substances, the first being chlordiazepoxide. It is a white-yellowish crystalline powder, readily soluble in water. Its synonyms are elenium, chlozepid, thymazin, librium, decadil, napoton and radedur. Besides its tranquillising action, it relaxes muscles and stimulates appetite. It is also used in treating gastric and duodenal ulcers.

Pharmacokinetics of chlordiazepoxide. After a single dose, 0.015-0.025 g is absorbed within 35-45 minutes, and the peak concentration is seen within 1-8 hours. The main metabolites are N-demethylchlordiazepoxide and the lactam. The peak concentration of the first is at 8-24 hours, and its half-life is 6-8 hours. Of the dose taken, 35-60% is excreted in the urine and 20% in the faeces. It can be detected in blood plasma for 2-3 days.

The conditions matter in isolating chlordiazepoxide. Chlordiazepoxide is extracted from an aqueous medium under alkaline conditions with organic solvents. Its metabolite, the lactam, is extracted with diethyl ether under neutral and acid conditions. That is, the isolation medium differs for the substance and for the metabolite. From biological material it is isolated by the B. N. Izotov method.

Reactions for detecting chlordiazepoxide. In TLC, a Silufol plate is used; the solvent is a mixture of ammonia, methanol, chloroform and acetone, and the spot is visualised with Dragendorff reagent. Colour reactions: ninhydrin gives a brown product, and Marquis reagent forms a yellow mixture. Fröhde reagent gives a flame-red product. Taken together, these results help in reaching a conclusion about the substance.

Spectral properties of chlordiazepoxide. In the UV spectrum, the residue is dissolved in acid and maxima are seen at 246 and 308 nm, whereas the solution in alkali absorbs at 262 nm. In the IR spectrum, in a KBr disc, there is absorption in the regions of 747, 1240, 1561, 1125, 1095 and 1220 cm-1. In the mass spectrum, m/z 282, 299, 284, 283, 241, 56, 301 and 253 are recorded. The quantity is determined by SP (spectrophotometry) and PEC methods.

The next substance is diazepam. Its synonyms are seduxen, relanium, eridan, sibazon, apaurin and valium. It improves sleep, reduces fear in neurosis, and in epilepsy is used with other drugs. After it is taken, diazepam and its metabolites are detectable in the blood within 2-6 hours and fall slowly over 18 hours. With chronic use, a steady-state level is established after 4-6 days, and N-desmethyldiazepam reaches its maximum on days 5-8. Of the dose, 60-70% is excreted in the urine and 9-10% in the faeces; the half-life of urinary excretion is 2-7 days, mainly as metabolites.

Isolating diazepam and microcrystals. It is isolated from a biological specimen with organic solvents under acid and alkaline conditions; this is the Izotov method. With ninhydrin it forms a yellow-brown product. With a solution of mercury iodide in KI it gives an amorphous precipitate; in a moist chamber, after 10-15 minutes, hexagonal plates and elongated prisms are seen. With the copper thiocyanate complex, small spheroids form, which in a moist chamber unite in 20-30 minutes into aggregates of crystals.

Diazepam: TLC and spectra. In TLC, ethyl acetate, 25% ammonia and methyl alcohol are used in the ratio 26:1.6:3.3, or chloroform and acetone 9:1. The spot is detected with Dragendorff reagent. In the UV spectrum, the residue is dissolved in acid, with maxima at 242, 284 and 366 nm. The IR bands are 749, 1325, 1485 and 1692 cm-1. In the mass spectrum: m/z 256, 283, 284, 285, 257, 255, 258, 286. The quantity is determined by SP and PEC methods.

The next substance is nitrazepam. Its synonyms are eunoctin, radedorm, mogadon and neozepam, and it was synthesised in 1963. Its tranquillising property is weaker than that of other benzodiazepines, while its hypnotic property is considerably greater. After a single dose, the maximum blood level of 0.005 g is reached after 24 hours, and more than 90% is bound to plasma proteins. Within 48 hours, 23% is excreted. In urine only 5% is unchanged, and 95% is metabolites, namely 7-aminonitrazepam and 7-acetamidonitrazepam.

Isolating nitrazepam. Nitrazepam is isolated from alkaline aqueous solutions with organic solvents. The specimen is left with oxalic acid, at pH=1-2, three times for 1 hour each. The centrifugate is extracted 3 times with a 1:1 chloroform-ethyl acetate mixture. Alkali is added to the centrifugate to bring it to pH=10, and extracts are again obtained with chloroform-ethyl acetate 1:1 in portions of 20, 15 and 15 ml.

Identifying nitrazepam by microcrystalloscopy. Besides the general reactions, specific microcrystalloscopic reactions are used. A 0.1 N solution of iodine gives needle-shaped dark brown crystals in 10-15 minutes. Mercury iodide in KI forms an amorphous precipitate. Potassium ferricyanide 5% gives prism-shaped crystals; other benzodiazepine derivatives do not give this reaction. PbI2/KI forms dark red crystals in 30 minutes.

Spectra and quantification of nitrazepam. In the UV spectrum, a solution in ethyl alcohol gives maxima at 218 and 260 nm, and a solution in sulphuric acid at 277 and 340 nm. The IR bands are 696, 1339, 1534, 1611 and 1695 cm-1. In the mass spectrum: m/z 280, 253, 281, 206, 234, 252, 254, 264. The quantity is determined by SP and PEC methods. In PEC, the cherry-red product formed in the Bratton-Marshall reaction is measured.

About oxazepam. Its synonyms are tazepam, adumbran, nozepam, praxiten, serax and serenal. It is a white crystalline powder, practically insoluble in water and readily soluble in ethyl alcohol and chloroform. Its pharmacological action is close to that of chlordiazepoxide and diazepam; it is less toxic than diazepam, with weak anticonvulsant and muscle-relaxant effects. It is one of the metabolites of diazepam; after 4 hours it reaches a high concentration in plasma as the glucuronide, and disappears from plasma in 48 hours. It is excreted in the urine as the glucuronide and in the faeces unchanged.

Isolating and identifying oxazepam. By the method of A. F. Fartushny, 3 ml of an aqueous solution of hydrogen phosphate is added to 25 g of minced specimen and homogenised, then extracted 3 times with 10 ml of ethyl ether. In TLC, chloroform-propyl alcohol-acetone 9:0.4:1 is used; the visualising agent is sodium thiosulphate solution, and the spot is yellow or orange. UV: 234 and 280 nm in acid, 233 and 344 nm in alkali, 230 and 315 nm in ethanol. IR: 698, 1325, 1129, 1711, 1693 cm-1. Mass spectrum: m/z 257, 77, 268, 239, 205, 267, 233, 259. The quantity is determined by SP and PEC methods.

The last substance is phenazepam. Its synonyms are phenorelaxan, elzepam, tranquizepam, fezanef and fezipam. It is a white or slightly light yellowish crystalline powder, practically insoluble in water and ether, sparingly soluble in 95% alcohol, with a melting point of 225-230°C. It is a strong tranquilliser, with anxiolytic and hypnotic action. It is supplied in tablets of 0.0005-0.001 g and 0.0025 g. Its metabolite forms glucuronides with glucuronic acid, and it is isolated from a biological specimen by the B. N. Izotov method.

Identifying phenazepam. In TLC, chloroform-acetone 9:1 or benzene-ethanol-diethylamine 9:1:1 is used. By Mune, Dragendorff reagent gives an orange spot, and in UV light an ink-coloured appearance is seen. Beilstein test: if a phenazepam crystal on a copper wire is held in a flame, the colourless part of the flame turns green. This indicates the presence of a halogen. UV: chloroform solution 320 nm, alcohol solution 230 nm. IR: 2896, 1655, 1432, 1091, 1035, 877 cm-1. Mass spectrum: m/z 321, 349, 177, 75. The quantity is determined by SP and PEC methods.

t: Phenazepam: UV, IR and mass spectrum
n: We now summarise the spectral characteristics of phenazepam. In the UV spectrum, the chloroform solution absorbs maximally at 320 nm and the alcohol solution at 230 nm. The IR spectrum is recorded in KBr and gives bands at 2896, 1655, 1432, 1091, 1035 and 877 cm-1. In the mass spectrum, m/z 321, 349, 177 and 75 are recorded. The quantity is determined by SP and PEC methods.

To conclude. The 1,4-benzodiazepines: chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, nitrazepam, oxazepam, phenazepam. They are rapidly absorbed, accumulate, and may cause dependence. In the Izotov method, acid hydrolysis leads to benzophenones, that is ACB, MCB, ANB and BCB, followed by TLC in benzene and colour spraying. For confirmation, ninhydrin, microcrystals, and UV, IR and mass spectra are used. The quantity is determined by the Bratton-Marshall method with PEC, or by spectrophotometry. As a check, you are required to isolate chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, nitrazepam and oxazepam from blood and urine, and to write the hydrolysis reaction.

We turn to the review questions. First question: explain the toxicological and narcological significance of chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, oxazepam and nitrazepam. Second: how is each derivative isolated from physical evidence, blood and urine? Third: write and explain the reaction in which 1,4-benzodiazepine derivatives are broken down by hydrolysis. Fourth: what chemical and physicochemical methods are used to identify chlordiazepoxide and diazepam?

The second part of the review questions is devoted to nitrazepam and oxazepam. How is nitrazepam identified in blood and urine? How is the identification of nitrazepam and its metabolites by TLC carried out? How is oxazepam identified in blood and urine? And finally, how are the colour reaction and the TLC method used in identifying oxazepam carried out?

Revision: excretion data. Of chlordiazepoxide taken, 35-60% is excreted in the urine and 20% in the faeces, and it is detectable in plasma for 2-3 days. Diazepam is excreted 60-70% in the urine and 9-10% in the faeces, with a urinary half-life of 2-7 days. Nitrazepam is excreted 23% within 48 hours, and 5% is unchanged in the urine. Memorise these figures by comparing them.

Revision: UV maxima. Chlordiazepoxide in acid solution 246 and 308 nm, in alkali 262 nm. Diazepam 242, 284 and 366 nm. Nitrazepam in alcohol 218 and 260 nm. Oxazepam in acid 234 and 280 nm. Phenazepam in chloroform solution 320 nm, in alcohol solution 230 nm. These values help to distinguish the substances from one another.
